To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

intermittent feeding (1) depressed relative food intake and relative growth rate in heavy-breed chicks, but not in light-breed chicks; (2) increased relative growth rate in intermittently fed heavy-breed chicks; and (3) depressed body fat concentration in intermittently fed chicks.
the heavy-breed chicks are able to compensate for the intermittent feeding by increasing food intake and growth rate, whereas the light-breed chicks are unable to do so.

intermittent feeding causes a decrease in food intake and growth rate, an increase in the relative weights of the liver, the pancreas, the gastrointestinal tract and its contents, a decrease in the relative weight and fat content of the carcass, and an increase in the protein content of the carcasses.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the metabolic and anatomical adaptations to intermittent feeding of a heavy-breed chick.
metabolic and anatomical adaptations in heavy-bodied chicks to the intermittent feeding regimen, and the effects of intermittent feeding on the body composition of the chicks.
the effects of a restricted feeding regimen on the metabolic and anatomical development of the chick.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, under the experimental conditions, the metabolic and anatomical changes in heavy-breed chicks were similar to those observed in light-breed chicks.

intermittent feeding of the heavy-breed chicks was accompanied by an increase in the relative growth rate, an increase in the weight of the gastro-intestinal tract, and by an increase in relative weight of the pancreas and liver, and by an increased relative fat content in the carcass.

the heavy-bodied chicks, which are more susceptible to the deleterious effects of food deprivation and which are less capable of compensating for the adverse effects of intermittent feeding, are more sensitive to the metabolic and anatomic changes of intermittent feeding than the light-breed chicks.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
intermittent feeding causes metabolic changes which result in an increased efficiency of food utilization.

the heavy-breed chicks, which are more susceptible to intermittent feeding than light-breed chicks, have a greater capacity than the latter for metabolic and anatomic adjustments to the feeding regimen.

the heavier the chick, the greater the depression of food intake by intermittent feeding, and the greater the increase in relative food intake, growth rate and gastro-intestinal weight, and the smaller the increase in body fat concentration.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the metabolic and anatomical adaptations to intermittent feeding in chicks are strain dependent.
intermittent fasting is a safe and effective weight loss method.
intermittent feeding is a powerful tool for studying the effects of food intake, growth and metabolism.
